newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr looking down barrel of rate gun.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr looking down barrel of rate gun.

text.p: The Australian dollar dipped at the midsession in immediate reaction to inflation data so benign it made another rate cut seem almost inevitable.

The key underlying rate of inflation rose 0.3 percent in the June quarter taking annual growth to just 1.7 percent from 2.1. This was the lowest rate of increase since the series began and, critically, below the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target band.

Analysts reckoned such over achievement deserved a reward and, assuming wages data Thursday were as subdued as expected, looked for the RBA to ease as soon as this Friday. If they were right, official rates would then be below those in the U.S.
Such a crossover would be an event almost without precedent and analysts suspected offshore investors, used to thinking of the dollar as a high yielder, would react badly.

By 12.15 am (0215 GMT) the local currency had shrunk further to US$0.7362/67 having already edged down to US$0.7370 ahead of the data in expectation of low result. It had started at US$0.7389/94 after finishing at US$0.7400/05 on Tuesday.

Traders said support was found at US$0.7360 and the reaction had been measured so far since the data were well in line with forecasts. Nevertheless, expectation and reality were different things and they expected fresh selling once the message sunk in.

"The best aspect of the result is the low rise oin the underlying measure which took the annual to 1.7 percent," said Nigel Stapledon, chief economist at Westpac. "That is comfortably below the bottom of the RBA's target range."

"This opens the way for the RBA to cut rates either before or immediately after its next board meeting on August 6," he said. Rates were last cut on May 23 when the cash rate fell to 5.50 percent -- matching the Fed funds rate -- from 6.00.
That easing took many in the market by surprise and tipped the dollar into a downtrend which took it from 78 cents to an 18-month low around US$0.7310 last week.
The dollar had found very good buying support at 73 cents and bounced as high as US$0.7440 on Friday in response, but the gains had been slowly eroded since as offshore funds bet on another rate cut.

The inflation figures alone certainly seemed to justify one. The headline consumer price index fell 0.2 percent, the first drop since Q2 1992, to take the annual rate to just 0.5 percent from 1.3 percent in Q1. With the annual underlying rate at 1.7 percent, real official interest rates were now at 380 basis points, not that far from the 440 basis point held before the easing cycle first began in July last year.
Analysts noted there was plenty of slack in the economy, with unemployment stuck at 8.5 percent, consumer confidence subdued and inflation expectations at historic lows and falling.
some were not convinced however, reckoning there were enough life in leading indicators to suggest an economic pickup was already on the way and another easing was simply not needed.
This argument was finding more favour in the forex market than the bond or futures pit were the 90-day bank bill contract for September was almsot fully pricing in a cut at 94.90.
The doubters cited comments from Treasurer Peter Costello in support of their "no move" argument.

Costello has seemed to be playing down the prospects for another easing recently and did so again today saying the effects of the last cut had yet to fully flow through and monetary policy was focussed on conditions 12-18 months ahead.
"This is sober stuff from a government that normally never stops talking about lower rates and has given the market pause for thought," said one dealer.

He noted that even if the RBA stayed silent on Friday, the market would be cautious about assuming the cycle had ended until after the board meeting on August 5. That in turn would probably keep the dollar restrained under US$0.7475 resistance.
But if August 6 were to come and go with no move, dealers saw scope for a serious rally given the whole world was short of the currency after selling it for more than four months now.
In that event a target of US$0.7570 was reasonable, they said, and the US$0.7640/80 chart area achievable.

Were the RBA to indeed cut the currency would likely test 73 cents again but much would depend on whether the money market began to price in a sixth easing. If it did then bears would be looking for the 1995 low of US$0.7070, while should any move be seen as the last the dollar could yet rally.
